Narrator.name: The Narrator
Narrator.profile: An older British storyteller, warm and unhurried, with a dry wit: someone reading a comic fantasy novel aloud by a fire to people they are fond of. Amused by the world and its institutions, never by the children in it. Has seen everything twice and still likes people. A light, well-worn voice with a smile somewhere behind it.
Narrator.style: Read in phrases, a little slower than conversation, as if to a table of friends who will laugh if you give them room. The wry line is usually the last short sentence of a paragraph: take a small beat before it, then say it quieter and flatter than the rest, as though it were obvious. Never lean on a joke, never laugh at your own line, never do a comic voice. When the story turns serious, drop the smile completely: plain, slower, a little lower, every word placed, no drama. Documents (a register, a notice, an order of business) are read the way a bored clerk would read them, which is what makes them chilling.

Wren.name: Wren
Wren.profile: Wren, fourteen. Quick, bright, generous, always scheming, and frightened underneath it all. Talks fast to stay ahead of the fear and makes a joke the moment anything gets too real. The story never says whether Wren is a boy or a girl: the voice should be young and light and not read strongly as either. A light British accent.
Wren.style: Natural and alive, never theatrical. Jokes are delivered as if Wren has been rehearsing them, which Wren has. When a line turns sincere, Wren gets smaller and quieter, not bigger. If a line has both, play the joke first and let the truth slip out at the end.

Provost.name: Provost Marrow
Provost.profile: The Provost: the head of the school, a woman in late middle age who raised Wren and cannot say so. Clipped, tired, exact, kind underneath and determined that nobody will notice.
Provost.style: Economical. Every word costs her something. Warmth only leaks out when she thinks nobody is listening.

Other.name: A grown-up of the school
Other.profile: An adult of the old school: formal, certain, used to being obeyed.

omen: This is the prophecy itself, carved in stone. Leave the storyteller's smile behind for this one line: slow, low, ceremonial, each phrase its own weight, as if reading something older than the language. No irony at all.
